lead: The Laplace transform properties are shortcuts. Instead of integrating from zero to infinity every time, you reuse a known pair and change it: add signals, shift time, shift s, differentiate, integrate, or convolve. Each rule also states how the region of convergence (ROC) changes, because the ROC decides which time signal belongs to X(s). These rules build X(s) for e^(−3t)cos(4t)u(t) in one line, and they work backwards from X(s) to x(t). Circuit analysis, control loops and filter design all use them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for X(s)=∫x(t)e^(−st)dt and the ROC, and the cosine pair from Unit 3, Fourier Series and Fourier Transform.

blocks.text: Write the one-sided Laplace transform as X(s)=∫<sub>0−</sub><sup>∞</sup>x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>dt. The lower limit 0− includes an impulse at t=0. s is a complex variable, s=σ+jω. The ROC is the set of s values where the integral converges.
L{a x₁(t)+b x₂(t)} = a X₁(s)+b X₂(s)
blocks.where: L{} means Laplace transform; x₁(t), x₂(t) are signals with transforms X₁(s), X₂(s); a, b are real or complex constants. The ROC contains the overlap of the two individual ROCs.
t₀>0 is a delay in seconds, u(t) is the unit step, and X(s) is the transform of x(t)u(t). The ROC is unchanged. The factor e^(−s t₀) is a pure time delay.
s₀ is a complex shift. The new ROC is the old ROC shifted by Re(s₀). Some syllabi call this the frequency-shifting property. For s₀=−3, replace s by s+3.

For the one-sided transform, take a>0 only. a is the time-scaling constant; time is compressed by a when a>1. The ROC is scaled so that s/a lies in the old ROC. The 1/|a| form with both signs of a is valid only for the bilateral transform, or when time reversal is handled separately.

blocks.text: Differentiation in time becomes multiplication by s, but the one-sided transform must subtract the initial value. The bilateral transform, with no starting point, uses sX(s) alone.

blocks.where: x(0−) is the value just before t=0. For the bilateral transform the term x(0−) is absent. The ROC contains the original ROC.
x′(0−) is the derivative just before t=0. Each extra derivative adds one more initial-condition term.
dX/ds is the derivative of X with respect to complex s. The ROC is unchanged, though boundary points may move. The minus sign is easy to lose.
τ is a dummy time variable. The ROC is the old ROC intersected with Re(s)>0, because 1/s has a pole at s=0.
* is convolution, x₁(t)*x₂(t)=∫x₁(τ)x₂(t−τ)dτ. The ROC contains the overlap of the two individual ROCs.

sections.h3: Initial value, final value, and reverse use

blocks.text: Two limit theorems read time-domain endpoints from X(s) without inversion. They only work when the stated conditions hold.

blocks.where: x(0+) is the value just after t=0. The limit must exist. If x(t) has an impulse at t=0, use the unilateral form carefully.
x(∞) is the steady final value. All poles of sX(s) must lie in the left half-plane, Re(s)<0, except possibly a simple pole at s=0. Otherwise the final value does not exist.

blocks.text: Use the rules backwards too. A factor e^(−2s) in X(s) delays x(t) by 2 seconds. A denominator (s+3) means a factor e^(−3t) in time. A factor 1/s means integration. For a rational X(s), partial fractions in Chapter 4.3 finish the inversion.

figure.caption: The tree lists the main rules; the orange s-shift branch is s → s + 3, which turns cos(4t) into e^(−3t)cos(4t).

spec.aria: A property tree groups Laplace rules, with the s-shift branch showing s to s plus 3.

examples.question: Find the Laplace transform of x(t)=e^(−3t)cos(4t)u(t). State the ROC. Use the standard pair L{cos(4t)u(t)}=s/(s²+16) with ROC Re(s)>0.
steps: Start with the cosine pair: X₀(s)=s/(s²+16). Its ROC is R₀: Re(s)>0.
Identify the multiplier e^(−3t), so s₀=−3 in the s-shift rule L{e^(s₀t)x₀(t)}=X₀(s−s₀).
Shift the ROC by Re(s₀)=−3: Re(s)>0−3, so Re(s)>−3.
examples.check:
a=3
w=4
print(a)
print(w)
print(w**2)
print(-a)

traps: Using s→s−3 for e^(−3t) instead of s→s+3. The rule is s→s−s₀ with s₀=−3, so the plus sign is correct.
Dropping the initial-condition term in a unilateral derivative: L{dx/dt}=sX(s)−x(0−), not sX(s) alone.
Forgetting that s-shift moves the ROC while time shift leaves it unchanged. A factor e^(−3t) shifts the ROC to Re(s)>−3 in the example.
Applying the final-value theorem when sX(s) has a pole in the right half-plane or on the imaginary axis. Then x(∞) does not settle to a finite constant.
Sign slip in the s-derivative: L{t x(t)}=−dX(s)/ds, not +dX/ds.

quiz.q: State the time-shift property of the Laplace transform and say what happens to the ROC.
quiz.a: L{x(t−t₀)u(t−t₀)}=e^(−s t₀)X(s) for t₀>0 (a delay). The ROC is unchanged.

quiz.q: State the s-shift property and give its other common name.
quiz.a: L{e^(s₀t)x(t)}=X(s−s₀). The ROC shifts by Re(s₀). It is also called the frequency-shifting property.

quiz.q: Why does the unilateral derivative property include x(0−) while the bilateral property does not?
quiz.a: The one-sided integral starts at 0−, so integration by parts produces a boundary term x(0−). The bilateral integral runs from −∞ to ∞, and the boundary term at −∞ vanishes when the transform converges.

quiz.q: Use the s-shift rule and L{u(t)}=1/s to find L{e^(−2t)u(t)}. State the ROC.
quiz.a: Here s₀=−2. Replace s by s+2: X(s)=1/(s+2). ROC: Re(s)>−2.

quiz.q: Find L{t e^(−2t)u(t)}. Use L{e^(−2t)u(t)}=1/(s+2) and the s-derivative rule.
quiz.a: L{t x(t)}=−dX/ds. With X(s)=1/(s+2), dX/ds=−1/(s+2)². So L{t e^(−2t)u(t)}=1/(s+2)², ROC Re(s)>−2.

quiz.q: For X(s)=1/(s−2), can the final-value theorem be used to find x(∞)? Explain.
quiz.a: No. sX(s)=s/(s−2) has a pole at s=2, in the right half-plane. The corresponding x(t)=e^(2t)u(t) grows without bound, so x(∞) does not exist.

quiz.q: A transform is X(s)=1/(s+1)+e^(−2s)/(s+1). Describe x(t) and explain which property creates the second term.
quiz.a: The first term inverts to e^(−t)u(t). The factor e^(−2s) is a time shift: it delays the same signal by 2 seconds. So x(t)=e^(−t)u(t)+e^(−(t−2))u(t−2).

quiz.q: From L{u(t)}=1/s, use time scaling to find L{u(3t)}.
quiz.a: For t>0, u(3t)=u(t). By the formula for a>0, L{u(3t)}=(1/3)X(s/3)=(1/3)/(s/3)=1/s. The two answers agree because scaling a step leaves it unchanged for t>0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Control engineers read stability and settling time from the s-plane using these rules before simulating a plant. Circuit simulators use Laplace-domain models of capacitors and inductors, then invert numerically. Search for Laplace transform in control system design, in circuit simulation, and in solving linear differential equations with initial conditions. The same pattern returns in the Z-transform properties for discrete-time systems in Unit 6.
